notes.meaning: Jesus went to eat at the house of a leading Pharisee on the Sabbath. Sabbath meals were usually special, but the religious leaders present were watching Him closely with hostile intent. Jesus still spent time with them to show them God's love and truth.

A man suffering from dropsy stood right in front of Jesus. Dropsy was an illness where fluid built up in the body and caused painful swelling. The man may have come hoping for help, or the Pharisees may have placed him there to test Jesus.

Jesus asked the experts in the law and the Pharisees if it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath. He saw what they were thinking and addressed their legal debates directly. God's law never forbade acts of mercy on the day of rest, only man-made rules did.

The religious leaders kept silent because they could find no commandment against doing good. Jesus then took hold of the sick man, cured him completely, and sent him home. His divine power brought instant relief without any outward display.

Jesus asked the leaders whether any of them would hesitate to pull a son or an ox out of a pit on the Sabbath. They were completely unable to answer Him. If their own customs allowed saving an animal in danger, relieving a suffering human being was far more important.

Jesus noticed how the guests picked out the most honorable spots at the table. In that culture, seating showed a person's social rank and brought public praise. Jesus used their pushy behavior to teach an important lesson on humility.

Jesus advised the guests not to take the seat of highest honor at a wedding feast. A more distinguished person might arrive, forcing the host to move the proud guest to the lowest place. Grabbing for honor often ends in public embarrassment.

Jesus urged guests to take the lowest seat when they arrive. The host can then invite the humble guest to move up to a better place before everyone. True honor comes when others recognize our worth, not when we push ourselves forward.

Jesus stated a kingdom rule: everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. God opposes human pride and lifts up the lowly. We are called to practice genuine modesty before God and other people.

Jesus told His host not to invite only family, rich friends, and wealthy neighbors to meals. People often entertain those who can return the favor, which turns hospitality into a selfish trade. Jesus wants our kindness to go beyond self-interest.

Jesus commanded the host to invite the poor, crippled, lame, and blind instead. These needy people cannot pay anyone back with an invitation of their own. God Himself promises to reward such selfless charity at the resurrection of the righteous.

One guest declared how blessed it will be to eat at the great feast in God's kingdom. He was referring to the wonderful banquet promised when the Messiah rules. Many leaders assumed they would automatically take part in that joy.

Jesus responded with a story about a man who prepared a great feast and invited many guests. A servant was sent at mealtime to announce that everything was ready, which was the custom of the day. The feast pictures the rich blessings of salvation offered in the gospel.

All the invited guests began making excuses to avoid coming. The first claimed he had just bought a field and had to go look at it. This was a weak excuse, since nobody buys land without inspecting it beforehand.

A second guest excused himself by saying he had bought five teams of oxen and needed to test them. Like the first, he could have tried them out at another time rather than at the dinner hour. He cared more about his daily business than the master's feast.

A third guest bluntly refused to come because he had just married a wife. Although the law exempted new husbands from going to war, it did not excuse them from everyday social courtesy. He allowed family life to become a barrier to accepting the invitation.

The servant reported these excuses to his master, who became very angry at being insulted. The master told the servant to go quickly into the city streets and bring in the poor, crippled, blind, and lame. When the wealthy rejected God's call, humble outcasts gladly received it.

The servant carried out the order, but reported that there was still plenty of room at the table. God's provision for sinners is so large that it can never be used up. Heaven has room for everyone who comes to Christ.

The master ordered the servant to go out to the country roads and hedges to urge people to come in so his house would be filled. This points to the gospel reaching out past Israel to the Gentiles, who were far away from God's covenant. The servant had to plead earnestly with poor travelers who felt too unworthy to attend a great feast.

differ.view: God's gospel invitation presses sinners so forcefully with warnings and urgent appeals that it overcomes all unwillingness.
Christians must compel others only through loving persuasion and heartfelt pleading, never through physical force or persecution.
Preachers compel hearers through earnest words and tears, while the Holy Spirit alone has the power to change human hearts.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine applied this command to the Church using imperial authority and laws to pressure schismatics to return to the Catholic fold.

notes.meaning: The master declared that none of the guests who rejected the invitation would taste any of his feast. This was a solemn warning to the Jewish leaders that refusing God's Son meant losing out on His salvation. Rejecting God's mercy leaves a person outside His kingdom.

Large crowds traveled along with Jesus on His way to Jerusalem. Many followed Him because of His popularity, hoping for earthly honors and political deliverance. Jesus turned to tell them what true commitment would cost.

Jesus said that anyone who comes to Him must hate their family and even their own life to be His disciple. In ancient speech, to hate meant to love less by comparison. Our loyalty to Jesus must come before every earthly affection and personal desire.

Jesus taught that whoever does not carry their cross and follow Him cannot be His disciple. In Roman times, a criminal carried the crossbeam on the way to be put to death. Following Jesus means dying to our own selfish will every day.

Jesus compared following Him to a person building a tower who sits down first to count the cost. If someone lays a foundation and runs out of funds, neighbors will laugh at the unfinished work. Disciples must think ahead and realize that serving Jesus requires total commitment.

Jesus described a king going to war with ten thousand soldiers against twenty thousand. The king considers the odds first, and if he cannot win, he sends an embassy to ask for terms of peace. In the same way, we must carefully consider what it takes to finish the Christian race.

Jesus concluded that anyone who does not give up all their possessions cannot be His disciple. This means saying goodbye to our hold on worldly things and placing them in God's hands. Jesus must be more precious to us than all our earthly belongings.

Salt is good for seasoning and preserving, but if it loses its saltiness, it cannot be made useful again. Impure salt that lost its taste was fit neither for the ground nor the manure pile, so it was thrown out. In the same way, believers who lose their true devotion become useless in God's service.

differ.view: True salt cannot lose its essential nature, meaning that those who are truly born again will never completely lose their spiritual life.
Salt can lose its flavor, showing that true believers can fall away from grace if they stop following Christ faithfully.
